purpose: Stop AI coding agents from producing generic 'AI slop' UI (purple-blue gradients, default fonts, cramped nested cards) by giving them a shared design vocabulary and a deterministic anti-pattern checker.
workflow_summary: `init` writes PRODUCT.md/DESIGN.md capturing brand & audience. 23 slash-commands (audit, polish, critique, distill, animate, bolder, quieter, etc.) apply specific design moves. A 59-rule deterministic detector (no LLM call needed) flags anti-patterns and outputs JSON reports, markdown critiques, and hook manifests that surface findings straight into the agent's loop.
key_mechanisms: deterministic rule engine (not LLM-judged); command vocabulary; hook-based surfacing into agent workflow; PRODUCT.md/DESIGN.md persistent context files
design_knowledge: Typography (default-font detection: Arial/Inter overuse), color (tinted blacks/grays vs pure gray, strategic accent use), spacing (cramped-padding detection), component patterns (nested-card anti-pattern), motion/easing dating heuristics
external_dependencies: none required for core rule engine; no API keys needed
execution_tested: execution_not_tested — static review only per Task D policy; CLI behavior described from README/user guide, not run
demo_quality: Described in third-party writeups (Chase AI, DEV.to, personal blog test) as producing visible before/after differences; independent third-party coverage exists beyond the author's own site.
strengths: Real deterministic rule engine (not just LLM prompting); works across 14 different agent CLIs; explicit anti-pattern taxonomy; hooks findings back into the agent loop automatically.
weaknesses: Requires installing an npm package; some 'anti-pattern' judgments (e.g. specific font blocklist) will inevitably go stale as design trends shift; execution not independently tested here.
security_notes: Core rule checking runs locally with no stated network calls or credential requirements; still an npm package granting filesystem/hook access once installed — treat like any third-party CLI dependency.
evidence_notes: README fetched directly (raw.githubusercontent.com); cross-checked against 3 independent third-party writeups found via search.

purpose: Give an agent a deterministic pass/fail gate for generated UI by comparing a rendered screenshot against reference image(s) and returning a structured, machine-readable verdict instead of a free-text opinion.

A 90+ threshold gates completion -- below it, the caller is expected to edit and re-run until it passes. An optional pixel-diff tool can be invoked for finer-grained diagnosis.

external_dependencies: none required for the core LLM-judged comparison path

purpose: Give OpenAI Codex a natively-built, modular library of design/QA/motion/accessibility skills so Codex output stops defaulting to generic 'good enough' web builds -- built Codex-first, with compatibility adapters added afterward for Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI.
workflow_summary: ~70 skills in the public core, organized into installable collections (e.g. 'motion-core', 'qa-production-core') covering visual direction (references, typography, color, layout, imagery), frontend implementation (React/Next.js/Tailwind/forms/accessibility states), motion (12+ skills: easing, GSAP performance, reduced-motion, React motion-library patterns), accessibility & performance QA (cross-browser, responsive, visual regression, SEO), content/copy, and handoff/maintainer safety (checkpoint workflows, revert guidance). Installed via a Python script (install_skills.py) with dry-run mode and timestamped backups; two self-reported before/after benchmark runs (Atlas: 19/30 -> 23/30; Signal/Matter: 23/30 -> 28/30) compare baseline vs. skill-assisted output on identical prompts/models/constraints.
key_mechanisms: modular, selectively-installable skill collections; install-time safety (dry-run + backup); explicit rubric-scored before/after benchmark methodology, self-labeled as 'repository rubric scores, not an OpenAI evaluation' rather than overclaimed; a 9-site 'premium-website-showcase' demo gallery
design_knowledge: Motion/easing language and jank-QA, accessible-component patterns (React/Radix), color-material-lighting direction, brand-voice-to-UI-copy mapping, hero/art-direction guidance, cross-browser/responsive/visual-regression QA methodology.
tool_dependencies: Python installer script; individual skills likely assume a React/Next.js/Tailwind-oriented frontend stack based on named skill folders
external_dependencies: none stated for the core skill content itself
execution_tested: execution_not_tested -- static review of README/repo structure only; the install script and individual SKILL.md files were not run
examples_available: yes (premium-website-showcase gallery: 9 confirmed local website/demo builds)
demo_quality: Concrete, specific: two named benchmark runs with numeric before/after rubric scores and stated methodology (identical prompts/models/constraints across isolated directories), plus a named demo gallery -- more evidence than most candidates in this pool, though self-reported and not independently reproduced.
strengths: The strongest genuinely Codex-first candidate found in this entire research pass (across both discovery rounds) -- real code-bearing skill folders (not prompt-only), a broad and well-organized taxonomy spanning motion/accessibility/visual-QA/design-direction, and an unusually honest benchmark methodology that explicitly disclaims being an official OpenAI evaluation rather than overclaiming. Directly closes much of this research's Claude-vs-Codex coverage gap.
weaknesses: Benchmarks are self-reported on only 2 runs and not independently reproduced; breadth (70 skills) means individual skill depth was not independently verified skill-by-skill in this review; adapter compatibility for Claude Code/Cursor/Gemini CLI means it isn't purely Codex-exclusive in practice, though it is genuinely Codex-native/primary by the author's own architecture description.
security_notes: Local Python install script with dry-run and timestamped-backup safety features per the README; no credentials or remote API calls stated for the core skill content.
license_notes: MIT (root), with a THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for public-core dependencies.
evidence_notes: README and repo directory structure fetched directly (raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com/tree listing); individual SKILL.md files within the 70-skill set were not individually opened in this pass, so implementation depth is assessed from repo structure, folder-name taxonomy, and README claims rather than skill-by-skill code inspection.
